note: Cuts are 10th/50th/90th percentiles from interventions/<id>_mc.py (100,000 draws, middle 80% kept). They are % of the per-visit factor in data/curated/intensity_factors.csv for that shop type, averaged over all shops of the type in a city. The percent is the trustworthy part; absolute totals inherit whichever pile they are applied to.

levers.title: Hotel water programme
levers.plain: Hotels put the “hang up your towel” card in rooms, and grants pay for low-flow showerheads, tap aerators and low-flush toilets.
levers.evidence_plain: Laundry formula from the EU JRC hotel guide with measured guest participation (35–49%); bathroom fixtures from logged US hotel rooms and two metered San Antonio retrofits. The share of rooms still on old fittings is unmeasured.

best_source.t: JRC, Best Environmental Management Practice in the Tourism Sector, ch. 5

dials: opt-out vs opt-in towel card (roughly doubles participation)
laundry efficiency (5 to 20 L per kg)
share of rooms still on pre-1994 fittings

cost_tier.t: $$ · about $100k a hotel, pays back in 2 years

levers.cost: ≈$100,000 per 400-room hotel with the utility installing the fixtures, payback under 2 years (EPA WaterSense, Holiday Inn San Antonio); showerhead $12 and tap aerator $8 installed (Illinois TRM v14 §4.3); towel cards ≈$0; laundry last-rinse reclaim $79,000 per hotel, payback 2.6 years (EPA WaterSense, Westin Riverwalk).

levers.title: Kitchen water retrofits
levers.plain: City pays part of new spray valves, dishwashers and ice machines for restaurants.
levers.evidence_plain: Per-device savings are metered (39 Massachusetts kitchens, 30 days each). How many kitchens still hold old kit has never been surveyed, and since 2019 every valve sold is already efficient.

best_source.t: DNV GL 2014, Massachusetts pre-rinse spray valve impact evaluation

dials: share of kitchens with old kit

cost_tier.t: $ · $21–88 a spray valve, pays back in months

levers.cost: Spray valve $21–88 installed, payback 4–8 months (Illinois TRM v14 §4.2.11, EPA WaterSense); ENERGY STAR dishwasher +$156–3,309 over standard, saves ≈$1,616 a year in utilities (Illinois TRM §4.2.6, DOE FEMP).

levers.title: Kitchen energy retrofits
levers.plain: City pays part of efficient fryers, ovens, fridges and smart exhaust hoods for restaurants.
levers.evidence_plain: Six sub-metered California kitchens: cookline gas −19 to −68%, exhaust fans −45 to −49%. A shop that takes the grant saves 12–21%; spread over every restaurant it is 4–9%.
dials: share of kitchens with old kit
grant limited to the biggest energy hogs vs any ENERGY STAR item

cost_tier.t: $$ · per-appliance grants, programme cost not pulled

levers.cost: Per-measure costs live in Illinois TRM v14 §4.2 (commercial kitchen equipment); no single programme cost pulled yet.

levers.title: Grocery fridge doors
levers.plain: Grants to put glass doors on open fridge cases in grocery and convenience stores.
levers.evidence_plain: 42 days of metering in two Kansas supermarkets: doored cases use 23% less, no sales loss. A store that signs up saves 7–13%; spread over all grocery shops 4–8%.

best_source.t: Fricke & Becker 2010, ASHRAE RP-1402 display case doors

dials: share of stores still running open cases
heated glass vs no-heat glass + LED

cost_tier.t: $$ · door kits per fridge case, cost not pulled

levers.cost: No public cost dataset pulled yet (retrofit door kits are priced per linear foot by vendors, not in the TRMs we checked).

levers.title: Cool roofs in hot corridors
levers.plain: White-coat restaurant roofs in the hottest districts when they come up for recoating; plant street trees as a legacy, not a 2026 saving.
levers.evidence_plain: Metered cool-roof retrofits cut 10–30% of cooling energy, and cooling is ~15% of a restaurant's July energy, so ≈2% of the visit for single-storey shops. Hotels save under 1% (only the top floor sits beneath the roof), so they are left out. Trees are excluded from the cut: a planted street tree needs 10–15 years to shade anything, and it costs irrigation water.

best_source.t: Akbari, Levinson & Rainer 2005, monitored cool roofs on California commercial buildings

dials: share of roofs that are single-storey and due for recoating
trees as legacy line (≈88 kWh/yr per mature public tree, USFS)

cost_tier.t: $$ · recoat at the next reroof, pays over years

levers.cost: No public installed-cost dataset (RSMeans is paywalled); modelled net saving $0.36 per m² of roof per year after the winter penalty (Levinson & Akbari 2010). Trees: $80–120 to plant, $20–34 per public tree per year over 40 years (USFS Northeast Community Tree Guide).
levers.card: interventions/cool_roofs_shade.md (research summary; no MC script yet)

levers.title: Event-week cooling setpoints
levers.plain: Hotels, restaurants and venues set the air conditioning 1–2 °C warmer for the event week.
levers.evidence_plain: 1 °C saves 7–8% of cooling energy in Houston/Miami simulations; cooling is 15–35% of July electricity. Pre-cooling only moves power to the morning, it does not cut kWh.

best_source.t: Ghahramani et al. 2016, Applied Energy (setpoints in hot US cities)

dials: event week only vs whole summer

cost_tier.t: $0 · a thermostat rule, nothing to buy

levers.cost: ≈$0 — a thermostat reprogramming protocol, no equipment; optional guest-room HVAC controller $260 per room (Illinois TRM v14 §4.4.8).

levers.title: Plant-forward concessions
levers.plain: Stadium food contracts make the plant-based option the default or the first thing you see.
levers.evidence_plain: Three US randomised trials at catered events: plant default +47 points of uptake. Not tested in a stadium; the concession menu mix is assumed. The shop data never sees stadium concessions, so this is attendance × per-fan, not a shop cut.

best_source.t: Boronowsky et al. 2022, Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems

dials: share of concession points that comply
levers.cost: ≤$0 — plant-based meals average ≈30% cheaper ingredients than meat-based (Bryant Research 2024); retail beef $6.32/lb vs chicken $2.40/lb (BLS average prices); the big cafeteria trial saw no drop in total sales (Garnett 2019).

levers.title: Free transit with the match ticket
levers.plain: Your match ticket is also a free bus and train pass, with extra service and park-and-ride.
levers.evidence_plain: Measured at the 2006 World Cup (public transport 40% → 57%), London 2012 and Super Bowl XLVIII, but every big shift also had a parking cap. Not in the shop data: attendance × per-fan.

best_source.t: Öko-Institut, Green Goal Legacy Report (2006 World Cup)

dials: with or without a parking cap

cost_tier.t: $$$ · about $6M a match for extra service

levers.cost: Extra service costs the host agency $165–352 per bus-hour depending on the city (FTA National Transit Database 2024); NJ Transit priced its 2026 match specials at ≈$6M per match; an electric shuttle bus is ≈$770–908k with charging. No per-rider subsidy figure is published anywhere.
